title: Professional Ethics in Aerospace Engineering
subtitle: A single session for third-year B.Tech students on how engineering catastrophes are produced by ordinary people following ordinary incentives, told through Challenger, the Boeing 737 MAX and Chandrayaan.
startNote: This was a single session, not a full course. The slides used in it are posted below.
modulesLead: Two decisions, and 353 people. The session opens by putting students in the room the night before a launch, then works through three cases and ends with what an engineer can actually do.

modules.title: You are in the room — 27 January 1986, 8:45 pm
items: The call, and the evidence you have
The same data, with nothing left out

modules.title: Challenger — how a known problem becomes an accepted one
items: What the O-ring had to do, and why the problem was not a surprise
The trap has a name: normalisation of deviance
The teleconference, and what happened to the man who objected

modules.title: The 737 MAX — how a decision gets made by nobody
items: It starts as a commercial problem, and becomes an engineering one
One sensor, and the months between the two crashes
Who was supposed to catch this? The problem of many hands

modules.title: The other reflex — the same kind of evidence, a different answer
So what do you do?
items: Four ways of meeting a failure
Three questions worth asking out loud
What you can actually do at your level
What the profession offers you, and its limit

references.text: Feynman, R. P. — Appendix F to the Rogers Commission Report, 1986. Six pages, free on the NASA history site.
Vaughan, D. — The Challenger Launch Decision, 1996. The source of “normalisation of deviance”.
Sterman, J. & Quinn, J. — Boeing's 737 MAX 8 Disasters, MIT Sloan, 2023. A free case study that takes the systems view.
Herkert, J., Borenstein, J. & Miller, K. — “The Boeing 737 MAX: Lessons for Engineering Ethics”, Science and Engineering Ethics, 2020.
Tufte, E. — Visual Explanations, 1997, on the O-ring charts, read alongside the published criticism of his reading.
